body:
Why regional differences matter

The Harappan decline was not uniform across the northwestern subcontinent. Some large urban centres lost their earlier importance, while other areas continued to support settlements. Gujarat is especially important because it provides examples of Harappan habitation and cultural change extending beyond the end of the Mature Harappan phase.

The principal distinction is between the continued occupation of a site and the continued existence of its earlier urban system. A settlement could remain inhabited even when its buildings, crafts and economic organisation had changed.

Dholavira: occupation across several Harappan phases

Dholavira is situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. Its remains represent Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases. The site was occupied approximately between 3000 BCE and 1500 BCE.

Dholavira is known for its fortified urban layout, extensive use of stone and sophisticated arrangements for collecting and storing water. Its long occupational history shows that an important Harappan settlement could pass through periods of growth, flourishing and decline rather than ending abruptly in 1900 BCE.

The occupation span of Dholavira must not be misread. It does not mean that the city's full Mature Harappan urban organisation remained unchanged until 1500 BCE.

Lothal: change after the Mature Harappan phase

Lothal in Gujarat was an important Harappan centre associated with crafts and exchange. Archaeological work distinguishes an earlier Mature Harappan occupation from a later phase.

In the Archaeological Survey of India's published sequence, the later Lothal B phase is dated approximately 1900–1600 BCE. This later occupation shows that cultural life continued after the decline of the earlier urban phase, although settlement organisation and material culture changed.

Rangpur and local cultural development

Rangpur, in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, is another important example. Its later occupational phases show changes in pottery while retaining connections with earlier Harappan ceramic traditions.

The development of local pottery forms at Rangpur illustrates regional continuity with modification. Cultural traditions could be adapted rather than simply abandoned. This is a more accurate description than assuming that every Harappan settlement experienced the same complete break.

Comparing Gujarat's examples

Dholavira, Lothal and Rangpur help explain different aspects of the transition. Dholavira demonstrates long habitation spanning multiple phases. Lothal provides evidence of an identifiable later occupation after the Mature Harappan period. Rangpur illustrates the development of regional pottery traditions.

Site continuity does not mean complete cultural uniformity. A place may preserve some Harappan practices while losing others or developing new regional forms.

Prelims focus

  • Dholavira: Khadir Bet, Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
  • Dholavira's approximate occupation span is 3000–1500 BCE, covering Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases.
  • Lothal: Gujarat site with a later phase dated approximately 1900–1600 BCE in the ASI's published sequence.
  • Rangpur: Saurashtra site important for later regional pottery developments.
  • Trap: Continued habitation after 1900 BCE does not prove that Mature Harappan city life remained unchanged.

[Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Dholavira: a Harappan City', Description and Criterion (iii), accessed 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955–62), Volume I, 1979, Chronology, pp. 24–45, including 'Revised Date of Rangpur', accessed 17 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, p. 17; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 4, pp. 39–40.]

title: Regional Transformation and Continuity in Gujarat

body:
What survived the decline of the cities?

Although the major Harappan urban system declined, its people did not disappear as a single population. Communities continued to live in different parts of the subcontinent, and some economic activities, skills and material traditions survived in modified forms.

The most important aspect of this legacy is the distinction between continuity of everyday practices and continuity of an organised urban civilisation.

Agriculture and animal husbandry

Harappan society already depended on cultivation and livestock rearing. After the decline of major cities, farming and herding continued to support many smaller settlements.

Earlier Harappan agriculture included crops such as wheat and barley, while millets were also cultivated in parts of Gujarat. The continuation of agricultural life is important because food production did not depend on the survival of large cities or their systems of administration.

Communities could adjust their crops and settlement locations to local conditions. This helps explain how rural life could continue even when the economic organisation of major cities became difficult to maintain.

Crafts and regional material traditions

The Harappans possessed skills in pottery, bead-making, metalworking and the production of ornaments. After 1900 BCE, the highly standardised and specialised production characteristic of the Mature Harappan period declined in many places.

However, pottery-making and other crafts did not vanish altogether. Later settlements developed their own local forms and styles. In Gujarat, the changing pottery traditions of Rangpur provide an example of this process. Later metalworking and craft traditions elsewhere in the subcontinent also show that technical knowledge continued to develop after the Harappan urban phase.

The continuity of a skill does not necessarily mean that the same workshop, organisation or exact production method survived unchanged.

What did not continue in the same form?

Several features that had distinguished the Mature Harappan urban world no longer remained widespread in the Late Harappan period:

  • The earlier common system of standardised weights lost its former importance.
  • The characteristic Harappan script and seals ceased to be widely used.
  • Large, planned urban centres and major public construction were no longer prominent across the former civilisation.
  • Extensive long-distance exchange and highly specialised production declined.

These changes explain why historians distinguish the Mature Harappan from the Late Harappan period, even though some populations and traditions continued.

Limits of claims about cultural continuity

Some objects and practices associated with the Harappans resemble those found in later Indian life. Such similarities can suggest continuity, but they do not automatically prove an unbroken history for every custom, religious belief or symbol.

The Harappan script remains undeciphered. Consequently, it cannot securely establish the names, languages or beliefs of the people who used it. Claims that every later Indian religious practice can be traced directly to the Harappans go beyond what the available evidence demonstrates.

The central distinction

Harappan urban institutions declined, but Harappan populations and some cultural practices continued. The Late Harappan period was a period of transformation and regional variation rather than complete disappearance.

The whole process in one view

The decline can be understood through 3 connected developments. First, environmental and economic pressures affected different regions in different ways. Second, the earlier common urban system weakened, as seen in the reduced use of seals, writing, standardised weights and major public buildings. Third, people continued in smaller settlements, including those in Gujarat, and maintained or adapted aspects of agriculture and craft production.

Prelims focus

  • De-urbanisation means the decline of the earlier urban system, not the extinction of the population.
  • Farming, herding and some crafts continued in later regional settlements.
  • Seals, script, standardised weights and extensive urban organisation became much less prominent.
  • Regional examples in Gujarat include Dholavira, Lothal and Rangpur.
  • The Harappan script remains undeciphered.
  • Trap: Resemblance between a Harappan object and a later custom is not, by itself, proof of direct and uninterrupted cultural continuity.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, pp. 15–17 and 23–24; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 102–103; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 2, 'Arts of the Indus Valley', pp. 10–11; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955–62), Volume I, 1979, Chronology, pp. 24–45, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: The Harappan Legacy: Continuity and Change
